intro: Welcome. In this lesson we study the society and economy of the Gupta age.

We will cover five parts: ports, trade and crafts; the decline of trade and towns; varna, jati and women; the guilds and the Dashpur inscription; and finally, what the Chinese pilgrim Fa-hien saw in India.

0.say: Let us begin with the ports, the gateways of Gupta trade.
Tamralipti, today's Tamluk in Bengal, was on the east coast. It handled North India's trade with South-East Asia, China, Sri Lanka, Java and Sumatra.
Bhrigukachchha, also called Broach, Bharuch or Barygaza, stood at the mouth of the Narmada in Gujarat. It was the largest port on the west coast, and handled trade with the West.
Kalyan and Chaul were on the Konkan coast. Chaul lay about twenty-three miles south of Mumbai.
In our own Andhra region, Ghantasala and Kadura in Krishna district were busy east-coast ports.
Sopara and Cambay served western India.
And in the south, Arikamedu, Kaveripattanam and Muziris carried international trade, including trade with Rome.
Remember: Ghantasala, Kadura and Chaul were ports that handled foreign trade.
Now, crafts. Textiles were the main export. The great centres were Gujarat, that is Lata, Bengal, the Deccan and the Tamil country.
Along with textiles, India exported gems and spices.
And it imported silk from China, which the texts call Chinansuka.
Vidisha was known for cloth and ivory work.
In Andhra, Motupalli and Koduru carried South-East Asian trade under the Vishnukundins.
And the weavers' guild of the Satavahana times was called the Kolika Shreni.
Coins. The Guptas issued gold coins called dinaras, in the largest numbers of any Indian dynasty. But the later coins had less gold in them.
Silver coins, called rupakas, came after the conquest of the Western Satraps, and were used for local exchange.
And for daily exchange, people used cowries, as Fa-hien noted.

One more point to remember. The Sudarshana lake at Girnar was built by Pushyagupta, Chandragupta Maurya's governor. It was repaired by Rudradaman, and again by Parnadatta, Skandagupta's governor. We know this from the Junagadh inscription.

1.say: Why did trade decline? The main cause was the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE. North Indian trade declined from the seventh to the tenth century.
Trade with the Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, empire went on in silk and spices till about 550 CE. It fell when the Romans learnt to rear silkworms themselves.
The Hunas blocked the north-western route. And the loss of western India cut the inflow of gold and silver.
After the rise of Islam, the Sassanid decline hurt overland trade too.
As the Roman market was lost, Indian merchants turned to South-East Asia. But this new trade did not revive the northern economy.
A telling sign: in the mid-fifth century, a guild of silk weavers left Lata in Gujarat for Mandsaur, and took up other professions. Demand for silk was falling.
Towns, too, declined gradually in the Gupta period. When Hiuen-Tsang came, Pataliputra had become a village.
After the Guptas, towns such as Sanghol, Hastinapur, Mathura, Shravasti and Kaushambi declined, and coins became scarce. This decline was marked from the sixth and seventh centuries.

The historian R. S. Sharma saw shrinking towns, self-reliant villages and few gold coins as the basis of urban decay and Indian feudalism. His critics point out that coins still appear in texts and inscriptions.

2.say: Now, society. In this age, castes multiplied into many sub-castes, or jatis. They absorbed foreigners, such as the Hunas who became Rajput clans, and tribes, through land grants.
For example, the Abhira tribe split into Abhira Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Shudras.
Peasants were placed in the Shudra varna.
The Brahmanas themselves were divided into many sub-castes.
A new caste appeared: the Kayasthas, the scribes and accountants of the land-grant bureaucracy. The prathama kayastha sat on town boards.
Medhatithi, the post-Gupta commentator on Manu, declared that Shudras were not slaves by nature.
The position of the Shudras improved. By the seventh century they were seen as agriculturists, and they could hear the epics.
But untouchability grew. The chandalas lived outside the villages.
And the Narada Smriti lists fifteen types of slaves.
In the post-Gupta period, the jajmani system spread: hereditary service castes served landowning patrons, the jajmans, for a share of the produce.
What about women? Pre-puberty marriage was advised. The svayamvara gave way to marriages arranged by parents, and widows were expected to stay celibate.
Women had no general property rights, but they controlled their stridhana, the gifts received at marriage. Katyayana even allowed women to sell their stridhana.
The earliest record of sati comes from Eran, dated 510 CE. It records the wife of Goparaja, a general of Bhanugupta. Sati was still rare.
So, in no age, Mauryan, Gupta or Chola, did women have equality with men. In the Gupta age, their status fell.
And one more fact: Amarasimha's Amarakosha lists twelve types of land, such as urvara, fertile land, usara, barren land, and maru, desert.

3.say: The guilds, or shrenis, were the backbone of the economy. They were autonomous bodies of artisans and merchants, with their own rules, seals and judicial powers.
Some guilds even maintained their own armed bodies.
They took deposits and lent money, acting as banks.
The head of a guild was called the Sreshthi, or Setti.
And a caravan trader was called a Sarthavaha.
The Dashpur inscription, of Kumaragupta the First and his governor Bandhuvarman, records a guild of silk weavers from Lata. They built a Sun temple in 436 CE, and repaired it in 473 CE.
Its praise of silk cloth makes it the oldest example of advertisement in India, sometimes called the world's first advertisement.
It was composed by Vatsabhatti, and it calls Dashpur, Pashchimapur.
Let us compare three records. The Dashpur inscription: silk weavers, and a Sun temple.
The Indore copper plate of Skandagupta: a guild of oil-men, who kept a lamp burning in a Sun temple.
And the Damodarpur copper plates of Kumaragupta the First: guilds acting as banks, and the town board.

4.say: Finally, Fa-hien. The Chinese pilgrim came to visit Buddhist institutions and to collect copies of Buddhist manuscripts. Interestingly, he never named the king.
He describes a free hospital at Pataliputra, endowed by the citizens, where poor patients received doctors, food and medicine.

He was in India from about 399 to 412 CE, in the reign of Chandragupta the Second. He came overland through Central Asia and Gandhara, and returned by sea from Tamralipti, via Sri Lanka. His account is the Fo-kwo-ki, the Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.
What did he see? A mild administration: no spy system, safe roads, and capital punishment was rare.
At Mathura, he counted twenty viharas.
But Kapilavastu, Gaya and Kushinagar were in decay.
The chandalas had to strike a piece of wood to announce their approach.
And cowries were used for daily exchange.

outro: Let us recap. Ports like Tamralipti and Bhrigukachchha carried Gupta trade, which declined after the fall of Rome. Castes multiplied, the Kayasthas rose, and the status of women fell. Guilds were autonomous and acted as banks, as the Dashpur inscription shows. And Fa-hien saw a mild and peaceful administration.
Now practise this topic's MCQs in the APPSC Group 2 app. Thank you.
